events.subtitle: artist talk
events.title: Zhang Wenxin: A Polytemporal Journey into the Porous Zones
events.description:
This artist talk offers a cross-sectional account of artist ZHANG Wenxin's long-term research in karst regions. It includes a concise overview of both her personal art practice and her long-term collaborative project "The Con(tra)cave" with independent researcher Duruo Wang.

Inspired by the sentient ecology framework and Daoist concepts of the body and cosmos, while integrating Geotrauma theory and Confucian Feng Shui, Zhang places her art practice within the porous zones of both geological and social terrains. Her research trajectory began in the limestone quarries of upstate New York, extended to the karst regions of Southwest China (areas also inhabited by ethnic groups), and reached the Jura Valley in Switzerland, a historical center for both timekeeping and anarchism. Zhang will elaborate on her passage through these apertures, using the temporal and the corporeal as imaginative media to resonate with hidden spaces that, though geographically distant on the map, are geologically co-synchronous. 

Zhang Wenxin (b. 1989) now lives and works in Hangzhou and Chongqing, China. She received her MFA from California College of the Arts (2013). Zhang conceptualizes her artistic practice as that of a "terrain constructor," wherein her objective transcends the mere re-presentation of landscapes or spectacles. Instead, her work endeavors to simulate the rugged topographies that characterize the interface between human and non-human cognitive frameworks. Through the integrated use of still imagery, video, sculptural installation, and immersive soundscapes, Zhang orchestrates process-centric journeys designed to engage and modulate viewer perception.

Her works have been shown at Shanghai Biennale (2023), Beijing Biennial (2022), Guangzhou Image Triennial (2011), OCAT BIennial (2021), MUTEK Electronic Festival (2022) and Breda Photo (2020). She participated in artist residency programs organized by Pro Helvetia, Goethe Institute and The Center for Photography at Woodstock.

events.subtitle: artist talk
events.title: Han Mengyun:  “Mirror Pavilion” & “Night Sutra”
events.description:
This artist talk will highlight Han Mengyun’s major projects, “Mirror Pavilion” and “Night Sutra,” by charting her artistic formation as she diverges from a Western-centric framework into the complex historical ties within the profoundly intercultural context of Eurasia's past and present. The broad focus of her research encompasses interdisciplinary manifestations of cultural dialogue and polyvocal aesthetic conversations, ranging from religion, philosophy, and mythologies to vernacular craftsmanship, textiles, and bookmaking. She will also share with us her journey of bifurcating into “Day” and “Night,” catalyzed by both traumatic and enlightening experiences of motherhood, as well as her subversive approach to questions of tradition, belonging, and femininity, informed by feminist theory, psychoanalysis, and Subaltern Studies.

Han Mengyun (b. 1989) is a Chinese-born, London-based interdisciplinary and multimedia artist, filmmaker, poet, and mother. She received a BA in Studio Art from Bard College and has pursued the study of Sanskrit at various institutions, including Kyoto University, before completing her MFA at the University of Oxford with a research focus on Classical Indology and Indian aesthetic theories. Her practice is metaphorically divided between Day and Night, exploring a wide range of themes from the decolonization of Eurasian transcultural hybridizations to personal and collective experiences as a woman and mother.

events.subtitle: researcher talk
events.title: Adeena Mey: In and Out of London. Afterall as Transnational Platform
events.description:
Providing in-depth analysis of art and its social, political, and philosophical contexts across various publishing and research platforms, Afterall’s trajectory from 1999 to 2019 has been described as shifting from a position of ‘criticality’ to one of ‘decoloniality’. Where does the project stand now, and how does it anticipate what is to come? In this presentation, Adeena Mey will retrace the history of Afterall, introduce recent issues of the journal related to East and Southeast Asian art histories and contemporary art practice, and discuss Afterall’s ongoing Art Writing and Publishing in Southeast Asia Writing Workshops series. 

Adeena Mey is Editor of Afterall Journal and a Research Fellow at the Afterall Research Centre, Central Saint Martins, University of the Arts London. His work explores contemporary art and visual cultures in East and Southeast Asia, artists’ moving image, and exhibitionary contexts in relation to cosmopolitical and cosmotechnical thoughts.

events.subtitle: performance
events.title: Anh Vo: Live Recording Session
events.description:
Transforming initial research into a recording studio, this performance distills Anh Vo's ongoing research into northern Vietnamese possession rituals. 

Sound Engineer: Isaac Silber

Strings: Jessica Pavone, gabby fluke-mogul, Ethan Philbrick

Voice: Anh Vo, Kristel Baldoz, Justin Cabrillos 

Anh Vo is a Vietnamese choreographer and writer working primarily in New York City, with a second base in Hanoi. Their practice fleshes out the body as a vessel for apparitional forces. Their work is situated in the unlikely lineage convergences between Downtown New York experimental performance, Hanoi performance art, and Vietnamese folk ritual practices. 

Anh Vo is a 2025/2026 Inaugural Fellow at initial research.

events.subtitle: publisher talks, workshop
events.title: Talks and Workshop: Book Making on the Edge – Publishing Potentials in Asia
events.description:
Happy autumn! September marks the third month of te editions’ fellowship at initial research. Throughout this period, te editions has been continuing to explore Asian publishing, especially focusing on its fragility, resilience, and potential. In thinking about independent publishing in Asia today, they have noticed that while each place is rooted in its own context, there are many shared concerns across contexts. These include how to navigate postcolonial legacies and censorship, and how to sustain production with limited resources and funding. Perhaps, one can glimpse something distinctive in Asian publishing through typography, paper choices, and printing methods, which reveal possibilities of their own. After participating in many international art book fairs, how do publishers from Asia understand their work in relation to the wider world?

This September, following the Printed Matter’s Art Book Fair, te editions will host an exhibition and an evening program on Asian independent publishing at initial research’s SoHo space. On September 16, te editions will welcome the founders of Reliable Copy (India) and Further Reading (Indonesia) to initial research, where they will share their distinctive practices through talks and a workshop.

Sarasija Subramanian, founder of Reliable Copy, will introduce Reliable Copy’s (Fine) Arts Dissertations Series, facsimiles of graduate-level college dissertations by artists from The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda (Gujarat, India), the first art college established in India post-Independence. Functioning as an early mode of artists’ writing which encouraged articulation, research, reflection, rigour, and documentation as key modes of learning within the largely studio-based programme, the dissertation was—and continues to be—a component which encouraged students to reflect on their studio practice and processes.

Januar Rianto, founder of the Indonesian publishing house Further Reading, will share from his own practice and lead a workshop titled Collective Index. In this workshop, participants collaboratively create the index of a book that doesn’t exist. Instead of writing the main text, they invent its back matter—entries, cross-references, and fragments that hint at what the book could be. This approach shifts attention away from conventional storytelling toward a speculative structure, resulting in a “publication” that is at once playful, critical, and open-ended.


____

Image: Left: Reliable Copy. Image by Eda Li.  Right: Further Reading Print No.4 Cover.

events.title: NiNi Dongnier: Process Notes – Every Motion is a Ritual
events.description:
Join us for an evening of Process Notes – Every Motion is a Ritual — performance screening, subtle dance, and painting by NiNi Dongnier, followed by a dialogue with initial research co-founder and artistic director Yuan Fuca on Friday, November 21, 7:00–8:15 PM. Limited capacity. RSVP via the link above. Following the evening, initial research continues as a studio, with Dongnier’s Process Notes on display between November 22–23, 12:00–6:00 PM. No RSVP needed.

me
right here
or only to you
conduct a ritual without theology
one verb after another
repetition
one verb after another, this is a ritual
can the meaning of a gesture, a sign be condensed into twenty minutes?
absolutely uncompromising
this is what I do
for you, my dear
for you, my fear

202509292350849
YXT: It's strange, so different even between evening performance and afternoon tech session. During the performance there is an “aura”; complete, extremely precise, and I can see progress in seeking truth.
202510061830135
MY: This piece is no longer like a dance. After one action, the next action appears entirely unexpectedly, and the next action is always derived from deep research rather than emerging from any habitual, inert pattern. It is a choreography.


NiNi Dongnier, Inner Mongolia-born and New York–based, is a choreographer and artist working across choreographic performance, moving image, and painting. She records and choreographs moments that hold intuitive truth and romance. Through movements and tactile materials that extend the body—garments, fur, oil paint, and technological interventions, Dongnier delves into questions about form, faith, constancy, migration, and the experience of life.

events.subtitle: performance
events.title: Ways of Floating
events.description:
Ways of Floating is an experimental ambient performance exploring how sound, breath, and cultural memory drift, merge, and reshape one another. Featuring three musicians from Hong Kong and Indonesia, the piece blends traditional instruments, vocal textures, and electronic atmospheres into a slow, immersive sonic experience — something between a live performance, a soundscape, and a meditative drift.


Musicians featuring in the performance: Olivier Cong（Hong Kong） A Hong Kong–based composer, singer-songwriter and director, Olivier Cong works across sound art, performance, installation and interdisciplinary collaborations. Founder of Raven & The Sea, his works span film scores, dance, theatre and operatic projects. In 2018, he was featured in Apple Music’s “New Artist Spotlight,” and in 2023 he collaborated with the Hong Kong Philharmonic Orchestra on The Wind with a Voice, showcasing his poetic and narrative-driven sonic style.

Nursalim Yadi Anugerah（Indonesia） An Indonesian composer and multi-instrumentalist from West Kalimantan, Nursalim’s work draws on indigenous cosmology, ritual practices, ecological critique and experimental sound. His compositions merge Kalimantan musical traditions with noise, chants and avant-garde structures. He has been featured at festivals such as Gaudeamus Muziekweek, AsiaTOPA (Melbourne), Holland Festival and TIME: SPANS (New York).

Special Guest (Hong Kong) Our special guest is one of Hong Kong’s most influential contemporary composers and performers, active since the 1980s. His work spans classical composition, experimental performance, improvisation and interdisciplinary art. He has created music for the Hong Kong Arts Festival, Hong Kong Dance Company, City Contemporary Dance Company, theatre productions and films. As the founder/curator of Music Lab and other experimental music platforms, he is widely regarded as a central figure in the development of Hong Kong’s contemporary and avant-garde music landscape.


This event is presented by See See Records in collaboration with initial research. See See Records, a project under the See & Sea Culture Foundation (501(c)(3)), curates live programs and collaborative performances in New York that span traditional, contemporary, and experimental forms. Alongside their event work, they operate as a publishing and documentation initiative focused on traditional and ethnic music from across Asia. Their current long-term projects include: • Amdol Tibetan narrative song (安多弹唱) documentation • Yi ethnic instrumental traditions (彝族传统乐器) • A developing series on Chinese Muslim musical heritage Together, these programs reflect their commitment to preserving regional musical lineages while fostering new cross-cultural and contemporary dialogues.


—
Image: Photos of musicians by Billy Elvis and Banyu Susanto.

events.subtitle: reading, conversation
events.title: Summer Kim Lee and Anh Vo: Spoiled: Asian American Hostility and the Damage of Repair
events.description:
Join us for an evening of readings and conversation with scholar Summer Kim Lee and our current fellow Anh Vo. Summer will read from her debut book, Spoiled: Asian American Hostility and the Damage of Repair, followed by Anh’s new writing on Vietnamese composer Ngọc Đại, before the two come together in dialogue.

Summer Kim Lee is an assistant professor of English at University of California, Los Angeles. Her book, Spoiled: Asian American Hostility and the Damage of Repair (Duke University Press 2025) examines how contemporary Asian American artists challenge expectations that their work should repair the wounds of racial injury. Some of her published work can be found in ASAP/Journal, The New York Times Magazine, Post45, and Social Text.

Anh Vo is a Vietnamese choreographer and writer working in the expanded field of performance. Their practice mobilizes the naked body in its variations to make visible the entanglement of power and apparitional forces that cut across flesh. Together with maura nguyễn-donohue and Lumi Tan, they co-organize We Exist in the Ambivalence of Those Motherfuckers, a program of residencies, performances, and public events exploring contemporary Vietnamese performance, hosted by Performance Space New York and the Center for the Arts at Wesleyan University.


—
Image: Cover of Summer Kim Lee, Spoiled: Asian American Hostility and the Damage of Repair (Duke University Press 2025). Cover Image: Julie Tolentino, HONEY, 2024 (Final Iteration). Performers: J Tolentino and Stosh Fila. Courtesy of the artist and Brown Arts Institute at Brown University. Photo: Peter Chenot.

events.subtitle: artist talk
events.title: Isaac Chong Wai: Biennial Commissions and Recent Works
events.description:
Join us for an artist talk with Berlin–Hong Kong artist Isaac Chong Wai, as he speaks about his recent projects, including commissions for the 60th Venice Biennale and the 14th Taipei Biennial. The talk will be followed by a dialogue with curator Kelly Ma. In the talk, Chong will share insights into two major works featured in these biennials. In Falling Reversely (Venice), Chong works with performers of Asian descent to study US CCTV footage of public assaults, using movement to slow, reverse, and transform these moments of violence into collective acts of resistance. In Touched (Taipei), etched glass and mirror panels capture traces of the artist’s own body, forming fragmented figures inspired by John Woo’s film A Better Tomorrow, its cinematic stills, and Chong’s childhood memories of Hong Kong, exploring themes of Asian masculine heroism alongside the subtle queer vulnerability within brotherhood.


Isaac Chong Wai is a Berlin-Hong Kong artist. Chong was a participating artist in the 60th Venice Biennale, “Foreigners Everywhere,” curated by Adriano Pedrosa and in the 14th Taipei Biennial, “Whispers on the Horizon,” curated by Sam Bardaouil and Till Fellrath. He uses glass, drawing, photography, video and performance as mediators to investigate contemporary global phenomena. His work transforms the emotions, tensions, and memories from human interactions into performative materiality and immersive experiences. His works have gained recognition at prominent venues, including the Biennale of Videobrasil, São Paulo; Bundeskunsthalle Bonn; MMCA, Seoul; Haus der Kulturen der Welt, Berlin and Liste Art Fair Basel. His works are featured in notable collections including Hamburger Bahnhof – Nationalgalerie der Gegenwart, Berlin; Kadist, Paris and San Francisco; Burger Collection and Sunpride foundation, Hong Kong. He is currently the New York Désirée & Hans Michael Jebsen Fellowship from the Asian Cultural Council.

Kelly Ma is an arts curator and writer based in New York. She has organized exhibitions and educational programs internationally to broaden historical narratives, including at the Asia Society Museum, New York; M+, Hong Kong; Para Site, Hong Kong; Queensland Art Gallery, Brisbane; Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art; Museum of Fine Arts, Houston; and Taipei Fine Arts Museum. Her work has been published in magazines such as ArtAsiaPacific and ARTCO. She has contributed to artist monographs and anthologies, including Hidden Realms: Korean Artists Today (ArtAsiaPacific, 2024) and Great Women Painters (Phaidon, 2022), and edited Assuring Our Cultural Legacy in the 21st Century (Asia Society, 2016), among others. She received a BA in visual art and history of art and architecture from Brown University.


—
Image: Photo by Andrea Avezzù. Courtesy La Biennale di Venezia.

events.subtitle: seasonal gathering
events.title: The Smiling, Proud Wanderers 笑傲江湖
events.description:
Join initial research for an end-of-year pre-dinner gathering, 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠, 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐝 𝐖𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐫𝐬 笑傲江湖. The evening’s theme takes its name from Journey to the West and later from a novel by Jin Yong, whose martial-arts novels shaped contemporary Chinese pop culture. Held in SoHo in the winter of 2025, the gathering is a small salute to people who move through heavy times with mischief, courage, and a stubborn sense of joy—today’s diasporic artists and art travelers. initial research will transform into a jianghu tavern—“rivers and lakes” in Chinese—a world of wanderers, outlaws, and those who live on the periphery. The evening will feature improvised performances by three folk musicians: 𝐙𝐡𝐨𝐮 𝐘𝐢 on pipa, 𝐒𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐃𝐚𝐧 on guzheng, and 𝐒𝐮𝐯𝐝𝐚 𝐊𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐢𝐝 with Mongolian long song. Artist 𝐃𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐧 will craft a special cocktail for the night, complemented by simple snacks for sharing. Feel free to drop by before dinner, stay to connect, or simply drift on. Tickets are available at the link above — all proceeds go directly to the artists.

👗 Dress code: Chinese chivalrous / jianghu-inspired, if you feel like it.

If you have any questions regarding ticket purchases or details about the evening, please contact info@initialresearch.org



Special cocktail by: Doreen Chan (b.1987, Hong Kong) is a mixed-media artist focusing on social practice. In her work, Chan re-examines the tensions between interpersonal relationships and subject formation. Through collecting, selecting, and reorganizing fragments from everyday life, she explores how individuals interact with collective and personal memories. She works site-specifically on installations, public programs, virtual projects, and collaborates with a wide range of individuals using images, sculptures, objects, sounds, and performance. Chan was listed as ArtReview China’s Future Greats in 2023. She was an Eyebeam fellow, a Delfina Foundation resident, and the 4th VH Award of Hyundai Motor Group finalist. She was also selected as Cultured Magazine’s Young Artists (2021). Chan currently lives in New York.

Music by: Zhou Yi (pipa)
Praised by The Washington Post for her “breathtaking” technique and expressive artistry, ZHOU Yi is a New York–based soloist specializing in the pipa (Chinese lute) and guqin (Chinese zither). Born in Shanghai, she began her musical training at the age of five and later graduated from the Shanghai Conservatory of Music. She is the co-founder and Artistic Director of the Ba Ban Chinese Music Society of New York and serves as an instructor and teaching artist at the China Institute in America and the Flushing Council on Culture and the Arts. As a featured soloist, Zhou has performed Tan Dun’s Concerto for Pipa and String Orchestra at the Gewandhaus in Leipzig, appeared in the New York Philharmonic’s Young People’s Concerts, and performed Bun-Ching Lam’s Sudden Thunder with the Sinfonieorchester Münster and Sisters of the Grassland with the Youngstown Symphony Orchestra. Her operatic and multidisciplinary guqin performances include Bright Sheng’s Dream of the Red Chamber with the San Francisco Opera and Huang Ruo’s Dr. Sun Yat-sen with the Santa Fe Opera. Dedicated to music education and outreach, Zhou has taught and lectured at institutions including Carnegie Hall’s Music Explorers program, Columbia University, and New York University. She served on the jury for the 2023 Astral National Competition and received the City of New York’s Outstanding Cultural Contribution Award for her impact on cultural exchange.

Song Dan (guzheng)
SONG Dan is a dynamic and accomplished guzheng musician known for her expressive artistry and technical mastery. Originally from Wuxi, China, she began studying the guzheng at the age of four and later graduated from Nanjing University of the Arts with a major in guzheng performance. Song has performed on prominent stages around the world, including the Grand Canal Culture Week in Brussels (2025), the opening and closing ceremonies of the World Fencing Championships in China, and the Washington, D.C. metropolitan area Chinese New Year Galas (2024, 2025). Splitting her time between Washington, D.C., and Wuxi, Song is the founder and Artistic Program Director of the Washington Guzheng Ensemble and the Executive Vice President of the Wuxi Guzheng Association.

Suvda Khereid (Mongolian long song)
Suvda Khereid is a long song (urtyn duu) singer originally from Shilingol, Inner Mongolia, China, who has performed in China, Japan, and the United States. In Japan, her concerts were covered by the TBC (Tohoku Broadcasting Company). In the United States, she has performed at the Chinggis Khaan Memorial Ceremony, the Brooklyn Culture & Art Festival, and the Brooklyn Roots Festival.

events.subtitle: artist talk
events.title: Asian Contemporary Currents – Talks by Five Asian Artists
events.description:
Asian Contemporary Currents brings together five artists—Julia Hung, Kenneth Wong See Huat, Nursalim Yadi Anugerah, Renu Savant, and Souya Handa—whose distinctive approaches span sculpture, performance, experimental film, ritual, and research-driven practice. In these short presentations, they share the questions and discoveries that drive their work. ​As current fellows of the Asian Cultural Council (ACC), these artists are participating in a six-month program in New York. This fellowship has historically supported the early careers of visionaries such as Yayoi Kusama, Nam June Paik, and Takashi Murakami. ​This event highlights the diversity of their perspectives, creating a space for reflection and dialogue. Through their varied approaches, the speakers illuminate the intersections of materiality, labor, identity, and cross-cultural exploration.

Speakers' bios:

Julia Hung (Visual Artist, Taiwan)
Taipei-born artist Julia Hung creates sculptural and woven installations that fuse Taoist philosophy, material experimentation, and the politics of domestic labor. Through everyday materials and gestures, she investigates overlooked value and domestic labor. As a 2024 Asian Cultural Council Fellow, she is in New York expanding her research on materiality, process, and cultural perspectives.

Kenneth Wong See Huat (Curator, Malaysia)
Kenneth Wong See Huat is a Malaysian curator, placemaker, and board member of ICOMOS Malaysia. Currently an Asian Cultural Council New York Fellow, his practice explores how heritage, queer embodiment, and everyday landscapes intersect through food, memory, and community mapping. Recent and upcoming works include his Medium essay “Queer Embodiment as Archive and Praxis”, his Pratt Institute talk “Art as Social Cartography: Tracing Communities in Malaysia’s Everyday Landscapes,” and his MuseumNext presentation “Forecasting Museum Through Community, Memory and Food: From Edible Memorials to Digital Cultural Mapping.”

Nursalim Yadi Anugerah (Musician, Indonesia)
Nursalim Yadi Anugerah is a composer and multi-instrumentalist whose work explores sonic experimentation rooted in the cosmology, cultural practices, and activism of Indigenous peoples in Kalimantan (Borneo). Blending influences from Kalimantan traditions, underground Indonesian noise, ritual chants, and European avant-garde music, all unified under the critique of ecological devastation and the question of survival. Through this fusion, he interrogates the intersections of ecology, technology, and decolonization, offering artistic pathways amid the urgency of Kalimantan’s environmental crisis. (more info: nursalimyadi.com)

Renu Savant (Filmmaker, India)
Mumbai-born filmmaker, Renu Savant’s practice includes diary film, short fiction, essay and documentary films. Chronicling lived time, personal and cultural memory and fabulation are at the centre of her practice. Set in the rural, coastal region of Konkan in western India, her diary and documentary films explore micro-happenings as unfolding real-time history. Her fiction set in urban landscapes uses story-telling and fabulation as a mode of expressing the layered political realities around her.

Souya Handa (Visual Artist, Independent Curator, Japan)
Souya Handa (b. 1994) is a Japanese artist and independent curator. Handa's works examine the intersections and conflicts between technology and society while exploring his Asian/Japanese identity. His previous projects have explored a range of themes, including gender, urban planning, and the history of Japan and nuclear power.

events.title: Display 2026 – Jumble, Tumble Public Rehearsal 1
events.description:
Display 2026 – Jumble, Tumble
Public Rehearsal 1

Performer: Tian Qin, Jil D.
Additional-Performer: Yu Ji

Doors open at 7:00 PM. Please note that doors will close at 7:30 PM, as the performance involves children’s participation.



Display 2026 – Jumble, Tumble for two performers, wood blocks, and electronics is a work that explores the temporality of thoughts and experiences. Through the tactile setup of woodblocks and the sonic interplay, actions accumulate, collapse, and reassemble, tracing the fragile line between order and disorder. The performance is a live process of redefining meaning from scattered elements, revealing construction and deconstruction as inseparable acts.

Performer Bios:

Tian Qin
Houston-based Chinese composer and keyboardist Tian Qin creates music that’s compelling, humorous, and visually vivid—blending text, craft, film, and choreography, often pushing the boundaries of traditional forms while incorporating her cultural heritage, engaging communal experiences, and guiding the explorations of body and mind. She’s collaborated with The Rhythm Method, Duo Impetuoso, Loadbang, Musiqa, Asia Society, and Roomful of Teeth, and is the 2024 American Guild of Organists Student Commissioning Project winner and a 2025 Houston Arts Alliance “Let Creativity Happen” Award recipient. Tian serves as a teaching artist at American Festival for the Arts, theory instructor at Opus One Chamber Music School, organist at Trinity Episcopal Church (Houston), member of Gamelan of the New Moon, and studies raga with Ragavan Manian. Alum of Shanghai Conservatory, Manhattan School of Music (BM), and Rice University (MM, Brown Fellow).

Jil D.
“I think I am an artist because I make books, & I know a lot of Artist. Jil draws and crafts.”



This work is part of BHKM and Yu Ji’s ongoing project Shack.

“When you enter the space of initial research, you will find a box standing against the wall. We call it Shack, a temporary body of sculpture that represents Yu Ji and BHKM: cardboard walls, painted radish red, cement flooring, supported by 3/8x3/8 wooden sticks, all walls open individually suggests alternative dimensions of the space that contains. Our materialistic practice happens inside and performative practice happens both inside and outside. The Shark employs method of ‘____’ and community building in order to circulate the idea of use “of”. Matters and happenings updated coordinately and improvisedly.”

— BHKM and Yu Ji

events.subtitle: artist talk
events.title: Glittering World, Unhurried Hand: Artists and Mothers in Conversation
events.description:
This event brings together two artists, Shouma Banerjee Kak and Jin Mei, who have each returned to art making in their fifties, after decades-long absence. Working autonomously and persistently, both have arrived at a practice of repetition, certitude, and joy.

Join us for a conversation between the two artists and mediated by their daughters: Chang Yuchen, herself an artist, and Amba Kak, a critical voice on technology and its discontents. Together, they will draw out what it means to return to something, to make steadily, to find in repetition not monotony but a kind of freedom.

Artist Bios:

Shouma Banerjee Kak
Shouma Banerjee Kak was born in Calcutta in 1963 and trained at the National Institute of Design, Ahmedabad. After graduation, she practiced as a graphic designer and illustrator across television and print. She has exhibited widely — a solo show at the Academy of Fine Arts & Literature, New Delhi (1989), another at Prakriti, Bangalore (1999), and a group show at Art Today, New Delhi (2001). After a long hiatus, she resumed work with a distinctive style of simple, repetitive strokes — a practice she likens to kantha, the needlework of Bengal, transposed onto paper. These works will be part of an exhibition in June at the Bikaner House in New Delhi.
https://shoumabanerjeekak.com/
Instagram: @shoumabkak
shoumabk@gmail.com

Jin Mei
Jin Mei was born in Shanxi, China in 1961 and attended the School of Art at Shanxi University in 1982. After graduation, she worked as an art editor for a magazine. In 1993, she opened her own business, Jin Mei Flower Shop, through which she supported the artistic practice of her family. In 2011, Jin Mei picked up a paintbrush again at the age of fifty. The book of her drawings, titled 晋美: jm was published by her daughter Chang Yuchen in 2024 under the imprint How Many Books. The same year she had her first solo exhibition at Kiang Malingue, Hong Kong, and launched a fashion collaboration with Home Society, Shanghai. In 2025, Jin Mei participated in a residency at Anaya, Jinshanling. In 2026, she presented her works at artbook@MoMA PS1 and Gern en Regalia.
https://changyuchen.com/jin-mei-1
小红书：晋美jm

events.subtitle: body practice
events.title: sensing periphery: body practice led by NiNi Dongnier
events.description:
We warmly invite you to a body practice, open to all, dancers and non-dancers alike!

Beyond creating work, our current fellow NiNi Dongnier would like to foster meaningful connections through a regular practice and artistic offering. In sensing periphery, NiNi shares body practice in an inclusive dance session.

Layers of practice:
- Awareness through gesture and the logic of moments in transition, deepening, and quiet transformation.
- Take our place in time and space, guided improvisations nourished by imagination and memories stored in the body.
- A material study of “Mongolian folk dance my mom created and taught me, but different.”

A note on the name from Yuan Fuca: we’re calling this practice sensing periphery, inspired by early morning light, when attention is soft, and the edges of things become perceptible again.


*Please wear layers and comfortable clothes. Bring a yoga mat or blanket if you have one.

**Space opens at 5:30 PM.



Artist Bio:
NiNi Dongnier creates movement sculpture grounded in the material study of gesture and the perceptual score of site and internal time, represented across choreographic performance, moving image, and painting, delving into form, faith, constancy, inheritance, migration, and memory. Born and nourished in Inner Mongolia, she lives in New York.


—
Image: Workshop led by Dongnier. Photo by Chris Randle.

When Light is Alive
Joy Li

Doors open at 7:00 PM.
Please note that doors will close at 7:30 PM.

This performance explores light in different ways. The artist, Joy Li, becomes a non-human creature by wearing wearable sculptures made of glass and light, using them as an extension of the body to interact with the audience. When light is alive, when it approaches, your pupils begin to constrict beyond your control.

The Shark employs method of ‘____’ and community building in order to circulate the idea of use “of”. Matters and happenings updated coordinately and improvisedly.”

— BHKM and Yu Ji



Performer Bios:
Joy Li
Joy Li (b. 1999, Gansu, China) is an interdisciplinary artist who works across sculpture, installation, performance, and video. Through her work, Li reinterprets the relationship between objects and the body, amplifying the allure and danger embedded in everyday materials. Her practice reveals how the material world manifests human desire, inviting viewers to re-experience familiar things in unfamiliar ways. She received her BFA. in Interdisciplinary Sculpture with a minor in Theater from the Maryland Institute College of Art in 2021 and will receive her MFA in Sculpture from Yale School of Art in 2026.

events.description:
I Split With My Friends, Taylor, and Chris

An exhibition by Sowon Kwon’s sculpture class at The Cooper Union

Opening Reception
May 15, 2026, 6:30–8 PM

Exhibition Dates
May 16–20, 2026, 1–5 PM (Closed Sunday)

Bereket Adamu
Muneeb Alam
Agatha Carlson
Dessa Ely
Ella Giallanzo
Jasper Krents
Sydnie Marshall
Hannah Muallem
Eric Nguyen
Nona Nishigawara
Mauricio Perdomo-Doncel
Gabo Sambar-Lande



A linguistic paradigm in sculptural practice was a point of departure, as was one Duck-Rabbit, and we went from there.

THREE WORDS:
anachronic grids, strata,
asemic, topographic, numinous,
equal-ish subset, misregister,
reiteration, reiteration, camo,
color balance, quartet,
formative, evanescent, splice
parallax, binocular, afterimage,
polytheistic, placeholder, metronome,
dayglo, vulnerable, bonfire,
bistabile, Saussurean treepaper,
in neutral, comma,
pathos, and, bathos,

AND A QUESTION:
How do you recognize when an additional gesture begins to hover, no longer requiring another?
What do the folds hold?
Is there a relationship between Genzken’s speculative interventions and Michael Asher at the SMMoA (now ICA LA)?
Have you had a chance to look into Maria Eichhorn’s work on value?
John Berger’s Another Way of Telling?
FGT’s ring of dolphins?
Are these viewing apparatuses and if so, what can they help us see that we couldn’t before?
If the canopy allows light in, what can grow?
Have you seen such a beautiful sunset since?
Are the ears-beak really a hinge?
Do owls visit you often?
“Morning, boys, how’s the water?”

events.subtitle: dialogue
events.title: Aging Out
events.description:
Join us for an intimate conversation between artists Yasmine Anlan Huang and Dahlia Bloomstone. From the dream of becoming an idol to the realities of affective work, both artists have navigated different social conditions while confronting the desires and expectations attached to youth and femininity: What's the difference between being desired and being loved?

Taking Huang’s most recent artist book, Becoming Everyone Everywhere (2026), as a point of departure, the conversation between Huang and Bloomstone draws on co-reading and comparative reflection on their similar yet distinct moving-image practices to investigate questions of ambition, longing, age anxiety, labor, and the ethics of storytelling, while considering how these concerns circulate within broader social and cultural frameworks.



Dahlia Bloomstone is a Puerto Rican/American artist and scholar and was a 2024–2025 Fellow at the Whitney Museum of American Art Independent Study Program (ISP). She thinks through social value, respectability, and moral regulation. She considers the politics around certain technologies, which function as stand-ins for deeper cultural and digital inheritances. She is currently most interested in “labor aesthetics”—in conjugating the surrealities of affective work.

Yasmine Anlan Huang (b.Guangzhou) is an artist and writer based in London and Dubai. Through the romanticization of and within girlhood, she explores how coming-of-age narratives become sites where desire and violence both reproduce and subvert colonial, patriarchal, and capitalist expectations. Across languages and media, her work further traces how stories mutate through processes of translation, circulation, and reinterpretation, seeking forms of resonance that persist across geopolitical and cultural divides.

Doors: 7:50PM
Duration: 60 minutes


Choreography: NiNi Dongnier
Performance: NiNi Dongnier, Zhengyang Zhang
Garment: NiNi Dongnier, Surgulen Mongolian Attire Atelier
Sound: Yi Xin Tong, Chingeltu
Lighting: Guy de Lancey
Photo and Video: Shina Peng
Curation: Yuan Fuca

Special thanks to Barnard Movement Lab, David Zhang, and Trajal Harrell.


————————————————————————————————————
202607011233422

In the reality of life that anchors me, I set this work off—the warmth and light falling upon my left eye in late autumn 2011, a glass of milk, a lump of clear tear fluid—factual raw materials move me toward abstraction, grounding and lifting.

My desire is to delve into the heart of concrete moments and things given, sculpting sensations into weighty gestures possessing purity, or the form of an immaterial spirit unbound. In the breath between migration from gesture to gesture, follow the innermost tempo. Each gesture bears my body’s entire history. A gesture is a verb, an act of a wish; even the slightest shift can become an event.

Not merely sex or love juxtaposed with death; vast natural phenomena are set alongside the subtle tremors of animal fur. I perceive these pairings continually welling up within.

Towards the true fact, to remember and fully feel its vibrations, I lean slowly, greedily into stillness, then bone-deep movement within that absolute stillness; humble, vulnerable repetition; compulsively tracking necessity and precision, until I can calmly relinquish control. With faith in the process of discovery, I learnt how to continue practicing, what dance, what choreography, what art means to me. This work is one outcome of that search, a threefold measurement and calibration: with nature, with life, with the spirit.

A work is a mystery. It has meaning, yet meaning should be delayed in arriving.

It’s that moment of incredibly conscious solitude, a rite for intimate gathering, simultaneously a quite reflection or simply rest.


————————————————————————————————————

Artist Bio:

Mongolian-Chinese choreographer and artist NiNi Dongnier creates formal and ceremonial movement sculpture and perceptual score variations grounded in the material study of gesture, intrinsic time, and site. Realized across choreographic performance, moving image, and painting, the work records and abstracts intuitive truth and the romantic, while delving into contemplation on form, faith, constancy, inheritance, migration, memory, and the experience of life.

She works with body movement and tactile materials that extend the body—garment, music, oil paint, charcoal, and navigation technology. Her practice explores the concept and construction of “performative landscape” and “every motion is a ritual.” Besides Fūdo of the Mongolian Plateau, her work is also informed by an art lineage that integrates her mother’s heritage—a choreographer and stage director renowned for Inner Mongolian dance and stage art, with Chinese folk dance, early postmodern dance legacies, Noh, and Tantric Buddhism, along with specific archival sources: personal notes, nomadic textiles, paintings, and dance notations.

Dongnier studied at the Beijing Dance Academy and has taught on its faculty, received her MFA from NYU, and participated in the Skowhegan School of Painting & Sculpture. She served as a tenure-track assistant professor at Simon Fraser University’s School for the Contemporary Arts from 2021 to 2024. She lives and works in New York City, where she also contributes curatorially to Barnard Movement Lab at Columbia University.
